title: Part 1, Chapter 37
paragraphs: Which continues the story of the famous Princess Micomicona, along with other comical adventures

Sancho listened to all of this with deep sorrow in his heart, watching his hopes of a title fade and vanish into smoke — the fair Princess Micomicona had turned into Dorothea, the giant into Don Fernando, while his master slept peacefully, completely unaware of everything that had happened. Dorothea could not convince herself that her present happiness was not all a dream; Cardenio was in a similar state of mind, and Luscinda's thoughts ran along the same lines. Don Fernando gave thanks to Heaven for the favor it had shown him and for rescuing him from the tangled labyrinth in which he had come so close to destroying both his good name and his soul; in short, everyone at the inn was full of contentment and satisfaction at the happy outcome of such a complicated and seemingly hopeless business. The priest, being a sensible man, offered sound reflections on the whole affair and congratulated each of them on their good fortune; but the person in the highest spirits and best humor was the landlady, because of the promise Cardenio and the priest had given her to pay for all the losses and damage she had suffered on Don Quixote's account. Sancho, as has already been said, was the only one who was distressed, unhappy, and dejected; and so, with a long face, he went in to his master, who had just woken up, and said to him:

"Sir Rueful Countenance, your worship can go on sleeping as long as you like, without worrying yourself about killing any giant or restoring the princess to her kingdom, because all of that is over and settled now."

"I should certainly think it is," replied Don Quixote, "because I have just fought the most enormous and astonishing battle with that giant that I can remember fighting in all the days of my life. With one backstroke — swish! — I sent his head tumbling to the ground, and so much blood gushed out of him that it ran in streams across the earth like water."

"Streams of red wine, your worship had better say," Sancho replied, "because I'll have you know, if you don't already, that the dead giant is a slashed wine-skin, the blood is the twenty-four gallons of red wine it held in its belly, the chopped-off head is the bitch who bore me — and the devil can take the whole business."
"What are you talking about, you fool?" said Don Quixote. "Have you lost your mind?"

"Get up, your worship," said Sancho, "and you'll see the fine mess you've made of things and what we'll have to pay for. You'll see the queen turned into an ordinary lady named Dorothea, and other things that will amaze you — if you can make sense of them."

"Nothing of that kind will surprise me," Don Quixote answered, "because if you remember, the last time we were here I told you that everything that happens in this place is a matter of enchantment, and it would be no wonder if the same were true now."

"I could believe all that," Sancho replied, "if my tossing in the blanket had been the same sort of thing — only it wasn't; it was real and genuine. I saw the landlord, who is here today, holding one end of the blanket and bouncing me up toward the sky very neatly and briskly, with as much laughter as muscle. And when it comes down to recognizing people, I hold for my part — simple sinner that I am — that there's no enchantment in it at all, just a lot of bruising and bad luck."
"Well, well, God will provide a remedy," said Don Quixote. "Hand me my clothes and let me go out, because I want to see these transformations and other things you're talking about."

Sancho brought him his clothes, and while he was dressing, the priest gave Don Fernando and the others present an account of Don Quixote's madness and of the trick they had used to lure him away from the Pena Pobre, where he imagined himself stationed because of his lady's scorn. He also described to them nearly all the adventures Sancho had mentioned, which amazed them and made them laugh a good deal, since it struck them, as it struck everyone, as the strangest form of madness a deranged mind could produce. But now, the priest said, since the lady Dorothea's good fortune prevented her from carrying on with their plan, they would need to invent or discover some other way of getting him home.
Cardenio proposed that they carry on with the scheme they had already started, suggesting that Luscinda could take over Dorothea's part and play it well enough.

"No," said Don Fernando, "that must not happen, because I want Dorothea to follow through with this idea of hers; and if this worthy gentleman's village is not too far away, I will be glad to do anything I can to help cure him."
"It is no more than two days' journey from here," said the priest.
"Even if it were farther," said Don Fernando, "I would gladly travel the distance for the sake of doing such a good deed."

At that moment Don Quixote came out in full armor, with Mambrino's helmet — dented as it was — on his head, his shield on his arm, and leaning on his staff, or pike. The strange figure he cut left Don Fernando and the others astonished as they took in his gaunt yellow face, half a league long, his mismatched assortment of armor, and his solemn bearing. They stood in silence, waiting to see what he would say, and he, fixing his eyes on the fair Dorothea, addressed her with great gravity and composure:

"I am informed, fair lady, by this squire of mine that your greatness has been annihilated and your very being abolished, since you have been changed from the queen and great lady you used to be into an ordinary young woman. If this was done by order of the magician king your father, out of fear that I would not give you the help you need and are entitled to, let me say that he did not and does not know half his craft, and was poorly read in the histories of chivalry. If he had read and studied them as attentively and as carefully as I have, he would have found at every turn that knights of far less renown than mine have accomplished far more difficult things. Killing some overgrown whelp of a giant is no great feat, however arrogant he may be; in fact, only a few hours ago I was locked in combat with one myself, and — I will say nothing about it, so that no one can accuse me of lying. Time, however, which reveals everything, will tell the story when we least expect it."

"You were locked in combat with a couple of wine-skins, not a giant," the landlord put in at this point; but Don Fernando told him to be quiet and on no account to interrupt Don Quixote, who went on: "I say in conclusion, high-born and disinherited lady, that if your father has brought about this transformation in your person for the reason I have given, you should attach no importance to it whatsoever; for there is no danger on earth through which my sword will not cut a path, and with that sword, before many days have passed, I will bring your enemy's head down to the ground and place the crown of your kingdom on your own."

Don Quixote said nothing more and waited for the princess's reply. She, knowing Don Fernando's determination to keep up the deception until Don Quixote had been brought home, answered with great poise and gravity: "Whoever told you, valiant Knight of the Rueful Countenance, that I had undergone any change or transformation was not telling you the truth, for I am the same person I was yesterday. It is true that certain strokes of good fortune, which have given me more than I could ever have hoped for, have made some alteration in me; but I have not on that account stopped being what I was before, or given up the desire I have held all along of relying on the strength of your valiant and invincible arm. So, señor, in your goodness, restore the father who begot me to your good opinion, and rest assured that he was a wise and prudent man, since through his art he found such a sure and easy way of remedying my misfortune; for I believe, señor, that if it had not been for you, I would never have stumbled into the good fortune I now enjoy — and in saying this I am speaking the plain truth, as most of these gentlemen here present can fully testify. All that remains is for us to set out on our journey tomorrow, since today we could not get very far; and as for the rest of the happy outcome I am counting on, I put my trust in God and in the courage of your heart."

So spoke the quick-witted Dorothea, and when he had heard her, Don Quixote turned to Sancho and said to him, with a look of fury, "Now I tell you, little Sancho, you are the greatest little villain in Spain. Tell me, you thief, you vagabond — didn't you just inform me that this princess had been turned into a young woman called Dorothea, and that the head I am convinced I cut off a giant was the bitch who bore you, along with other nonsense that threw me into the worst confusion I have ever known in all my life? I swear" — and here he looked up at heaven and ground his teeth — "I have half a mind to do such damage to you as will teach sense, from now on, to every lying squire of a knight-errant in the world."

"Calm yourself, your worship, señor," Sancho answered, "for it may well be that I was mistaken about the transformation of the lady princess Micomicona. But as for the giant's head — or at any rate the stabbing of the wine-skins, and the blood being red wine — I am making no mistake there, as sure as God exists; because the wounded skins are lying right there at the head of your worship's bed, and the red wine has turned the room into a lake. If you don't believe it, you'll see when the eggs come to be fried — I mean, when his worship the landlord demands payment for all the damages. As for the rest, I am glad with all my heart that her ladyship the queen is just as she was, because it concerns me as much as it does anyone."
"I tell you again, Sancho, you are a fool," said Don Quixote. "Forgive me, and let that be the end of it."

"That is the end of it," said Don Fernando; "let us say no more about it. And since her ladyship the princess proposes to set out tomorrow, because today it is too late, so be it; we will spend the night in pleasant conversation, and tomorrow we will all accompany Señor Don Quixote, because we want to witness the valiant and unmatched deeds he is going to perform in the course of this mighty enterprise he has undertaken."

"It is I who shall serve and accompany you," said Don Quixote; "and I am deeply grateful for the favor you are granting me and the good opinion you hold of me, which I will strive to live up to, or it will cost me my life — or even more, if it could possibly cost me more."

Don Quixote and Don Fernando exchanged many compliments and courtesies, but they were cut short by a traveler who entered the inn at that moment, and whose clothing suggested a Christian recently arrived from Moorish territory: he wore a short-skirted coat of blue cloth with half-sleeves and no collar, breeches also of blue cloth, a cap of the same color, yellow buskins, and a Moorish cutlass hanging from a strap slung across his chest. Behind him, riding a donkey, came a woman dressed in Moorish style, her face veiled, a scarf on her head, wearing a small brocaded cap and a mantle that covered her from her shoulders to her feet. The man had a sturdy, well-proportioned build; he was a little over forty, somewhat dark in complexion, with a long mustache and a full beard — in short, his appearance was such that, had he been well dressed, anyone would have taken him for a person of quality and good birth. On entering he asked for a room, and when they told him there was none in the inn, he seemed distressed; going over to the woman whose dress marked her as a Moor, he lifted her down from the saddle in his arms. Luscinda, Dorothea, the landlady, her daughter, and Maritornes, drawn by the strange outfit — entirely new to them — gathered around her; and Dorothea, who was always kind, courteous, and quick-witted, seeing that both the woman and the man escorting her were upset at not finding a room, said to her, "Don't be troubled, señora, by the discomfort and lack of luxuries here, for that is the way of roadside inns. Still, if you would care to share our lodging with us" — pointing to Luscinda — "you have perhaps found worse accommodation in the course of your journey."

The veiled lady made no reply to this; all she did was rise from her seat, cross her hands over her chest, bow her head, and bend her body as a sign that she was giving thanks. From her silence they concluded that she must certainly be a Moor, unable to speak a Christian language.

At this point the captive came up, having been occupied with other matters until then, and seeing them all standing around his companion while she made no reply to anything they said to her, he explained, "Ladies, this young woman barely understands my language and can speak nothing but the tongue of her own country, which is why she does not and cannot answer what has been asked of her."

"Nothing has been asked of her," Luscinda answered. "She has only been offered our company for the evening and a share of the quarters we are using, where she will be made as comfortable as the circumstances allow — with the goodwill we owe to all strangers in need of it, especially when the one being helped is a woman."

"On her behalf and my own, señora," the captive replied, "I kiss your hands, and I value highly, as I should, the favor you have offered — one which, on such an occasion and coming from persons of your evident standing, is plainly a very great one."
"Tell me, señor," said Dorothea, "is this lady a Christian or a Moor? Her dress and her silence lead us to suspect that she is what we wish she were not."
"In dress and on the outside," he said, "she is a Moor, but at heart she is a thoroughly good Christian, for she has the deepest desire to become one."
"Then she has not been baptized?" Luscinda asked.

"There has been no opportunity for that," the captive replied, "since she left Algiers, her native country and home; and so far she has not found herself in any danger of death so immediate as to make it necessary to baptize her before she has been instructed in all the ceremonies our holy mother Church requires. But, God willing, she will before long be baptized with the solemnity she deserves — a solemnity greater than her dress, or mine, would suggest."

These words made everyone who heard him eager to know who the Moorish lady and the captive were, but no one cared to ask just then, since it was clearly a better moment to help them rest than to question them about their lives. Dorothea took the Moorish lady by the hand, led her to a seat beside her own, and asked her to remove her veil. She looked at the captive as if asking him what they meant and what she should do. He told her in Arabic that they were asking her to take off her veil, and at that she removed it and revealed a face so lovely that to Dorothea she seemed more beautiful than Luscinda, and to Luscinda more beautiful than Dorothea, and all the onlookers felt that if any beauty could rival those two women's, it was the Moorish lady's — and some were even inclined to give her the edge. And since it is the privilege and charm of beauty to win hearts and attract goodwill, everyone immediately became eager to show kindness and attention to the lovely Moor.

Don Fernando asked the captive what her name was, and he answered that it was Lela Zoraida; but the moment she heard him, she guessed what the Christian had asked and said quickly, with some displeasure and force, "No, not Zoraida — Maria, Maria!" letting them understand that her name was "Maria" and not "Zoraida." These words, and the touching earnestness with which she spoke them, drew more than one tear from some of the listeners — particularly the women, who are tender-hearted and compassionate by nature. Luscinda embraced her affectionately and said, "Yes, yes — Maria, Maria," to which the Moorish lady replied, "Yes, yes, Maria; Zoraida macange," which means "not Zoraida."

Night was now coming on, and on the orders of Don Fernando's companions the landlord had taken care and trouble to prepare for them the best supper he could manage. When the hour arrived, they all sat down at a long table like one in a refectory — there was no round or square table in the inn — and the seat of honor at its head, though he tried to refuse it, they gave to Don Quixote, who asked the lady Micomicona to sit at his side, since he was her protector. Luscinda and Zoraida took the places next to her; opposite them sat Don Fernando and Cardenio, then the captive and the other gentlemen; and beside the ladies sat the priest and the barber. And so they ate their supper in high spirits, which rose even higher when they saw Don Quixote stop eating and — moved by an impulse like the one that had prompted his long speech when he dined with the goatherds — begin to address them:

"Truly, gentlemen, when you stop to think about it, the things witnessed by those who profess the order of knight-errantry are great and marvelous. Tell me: what person in this world, walking through the gate of this castle right now and seeing us as we sit here, would suppose or imagine that we are what we actually are? Who would say that this lady beside me is the great queen we all know her to be, or that I am that Knight of the Rueful Countenance whose name is trumpeted far and wide by the mouth of Fame? There can be no doubt, then, that this art and calling surpasses every other that human beings have invented, and deserves all the more honor the more it is exposed to danger. Away with anyone who claims that letters take precedence over arms; I will tell such people, whoever they may be, that they do not know what they are talking about. The reason such people usually give, and chiefly rely on, is that the labors of the mind are greater than those of the body, and that arms employ the body alone — as though the calling were a porter's trade, requiring nothing more than sturdy strength; or as though what we who profess them call arms did not include feats of vigor that demand high intelligence to carry out; or as though the mind of the warrior who has an army, or the defense of a city, in his charge did not exert itself as much as his body does. Consider whether bodily strength alone can discover or guess the enemy's intentions, his plans, his stratagems, his obstacles, or ward off looming dangers — all these are operations of the mind, in which the body plays no part whatsoever. Since arms, then, require mind just as much as letters do, let us now see which of the two minds — the scholar's or the warrior's — has the most work to do; and this will be settled by the end and goal each one aims at, for the purpose that aims at the nobler object is the more to be esteemed. The end and goal of letters — I am not speaking now of divine letters, whose aim is to lift and guide the soul to Heaven, for with an end so infinite no other can be compared — I am speaking of human letters, whose end is to establish distributive justice, to give every man what is his, and to see and make sure that good laws are observed: an end that is certainly noble, lofty, and worthy of great praise, but not of such praise as is owed to the end pursued by arms, whose object and purpose is peace, the greatest good that human beings can desire in this life. The first good news the world and mankind ever received was the news the angels brought on the night that was our day, when they sang in the air, 'Glory to God in the highest, and peace on earth to men of good-will'; and the greeting that the great Master of heaven and earth taught his disciples and chosen followers to use when entering any house was to say, 'Peace be on this house'; and many other times he said to them, 'My peace I give unto you, my peace I leave you, peace be with you' — a jewel and a precious gift, given and left by such a hand, a jewel without which there can be no happiness either on earth or in heaven. This peace is the true end of war — and war is simply another name for arms. Granting, then, that the end of war is peace, and that in this it has the advantage over the end of letters, let us turn now to the bodily hardships of the man of letters and those of the man who follows the profession of arms, and see which are the greater."

Don Quixote delivered his speech in such a manner, and in such well-chosen language, that for the moment none of his listeners could possibly take him for a madman; on the contrary, since most of them were gentlemen, to whom arms belong by birthright, they listened to him with great pleasure as he continued: "Here, then, I say, is what the student has to endure. First of all, poverty — not that all students are poor, but to put the case in its most extreme form — and once I have said that he endures poverty, I think nothing more needs to be said about his hard lot, for whoever is poor has no share in the good things of life. He suffers this poverty in various forms: hunger, or cold, or lack of clothing, or all of them at once. Even so, it is never so extreme that he gets nothing at all to eat, though the meal may come at odd hours and from the leftovers of the rich; for the deepest misery of students is what they themselves call 'going out for soup,' and there is always some neighbor's brazier or hearth for them which, if it does not warm them, at least takes the edge off the cold; and finally, at night they sleep in comfort under a roof. I will not go into other details — the shortage of shirts, for instance, and the absence of any surplus of shoes, the thin and threadbare clothing, and the way they gorge themselves to bursting when good luck happens to set a banquet of some kind before them. By this road I have described — rough and hard, stumbling here, falling there, getting up only to fall again — they reach the rank they desire; and once that is attained, we have seen many of them who, having passed through these Syrtes and Scyllas and Charybdises as though carried flying on the wings of favoring fortune — we have seen them, I say, ruling and governing the world from a chair, their hunger turned to plenty, their cold to comfort, their nakedness to fine clothing, their sleep on a mat to rest in holland sheets and damask: the justly earned reward of their virtue. But when set against and compared with what the warrior endures, everything they have endured falls far short of it, as I am now about to show."
